![Complete small-data EM workflow diagram. The labelled EM data (20–200 images) feeds augmentation and transfer learning in parallel; synthetic data feeds domain adaptation; all three converge on a fine-tuned model. The active learning loop (dotted arrow, bottom) queries the fine-tuned model for the most uncertain unlabelled images, sends them to expert annotation, and grows the labelled pool.](img/small_data_workflow.png){width="85%"}

:::: {.notes}
- Walk through the diagram explicitly: "We start with a very small labelled set. Simultaneously: augmentation manufactures more views of those labels; transfer learning imports features from ImageNet or a materials-pretrained model; synthetic Voronoi data provides thousands of free labels for pre-training. All three converge on one fine-tuned model. The active learning loop (dotted) then asks the model 'which unlabelled images are you least confident about?' and sends those to the expert annotator first."
- The one point to land: these are not alternatives — they are stacked. Every production EM segmentation pipeline uses at least two of the three legs. The strongest pipelines use all three.
- Misconception to preempt: "I should pick the strategy that matches my situation." Wrong framing. The three strategies are orthogonal and composable — they do not compete. Adding any one of them strictly improves over baseline; adding all three multiplies the benefit.
- Self-supervised pretraining (SimCLR/MAE/DINO, earlier today) plugs into the transfer leg of this diagram: it replaces the ImageNet backbone by one pretrained on your own unlabelled micrographs.
::::

## Validation in the small-data regime

:::: {.incremental}
- **Group by specimen, not by crop:** if crops from the same EM specimen appear in both train and test, the model memorises specimen identity (detector vignette, brightness baseline, session contrast) rather than the physical microstructure.
- **The protocol:** `GroupKFold(n_splits=5).split(X, y, groups=specimen_ids)` — entire specimens are in either train or test, never both. This is the Week 4 lesson applied to the augmented EM context.
- **Augmentation leakage:** if you augment before splitting, a rotated copy of a training image lands in the test set. The test accuracy measures memorisation recall, not generalisation. Rule: **split first, then augment**.
- **Honest consequence:** group-based splitting gives *lower and noisier* numbers — with 5 specimens your effective test set is 2 specimens. That lower honest number beats a higher leaked one every time. The variance is information (it tells you how little you actually know), not a problem to optimise away.
::::

:::: {.notes}
- Connect to Week 4 explicitly: "GroupKFold was introduced in Week 4 as the correct strategy for EM validation. Today's small-data context makes the leakage problem even more severe: with only 50 images, one leaked specimen can inflate accuracy by 15–20 percentage points."
- The one point to land: the split ordering is the single most important hygiene rule. Split-first, augment-second. Write it on the board.
- EM anchor: five specimens × 10 crops = 50 images. Wrong: 40/10 random split → every specimen on both sides → model learns specimen identity. Right: 3 specimens (30 crops) / 2 specimens (20 crops) → model never sees any crop from test specimens during training. Then augment the 30 crops to 300+.
- Transition: "Now put it all together."
::::

## Practical checklist for small-data EM tasks

:::: {.incremental}
- **Before augmenting:** confirm each transform is physically valid for your specific material and task. If the label is calibrated to intensity, brightness jitter is illegal.
- **Always GroupKFold by specimen** (not by crop): split first, then augment. A rotated copy of a training specimen must not appear in the test set.
- **Start with a frozen embedding + linear probe** (<100 labels): pretrained (DINOv2, μSAM encoder) or self-supervised on your own unlabelled images. Check kNN neighbours first. Move to LP→fine-tuning with differential LRs only if it beats the probe.
- **Synthetic pre-training:** if you have a physical model of your microstructure, generate 1 000–10 000 synthetic images first. Even simple Voronoi geometry pre-training helps if the task depends on topology.
- **Fine-tune with differential LRs:** backbone lr $\approx 10^{-5}$, head lr $\approx 10^{-3}$. Use gradual unfreezing (head → last block → deeper blocks).
- **Active learning + SAM-assisted annotation:** if you can acquire unlabelled images cheaply, prioritise annotation budget on the most uncertain/diverse ones and annotate with clicks, not polygons.
::::

:::: {.notes}
- Use this as the practical recipe students will carry into their miniproject. Point out that the first two bullets are *validation hygiene* that overrides everything else — a perfect three-strategy pipeline with a leaky split produces a confidently wrong model.
- The one point to land: GroupKFold by specimen is not optional hygiene — it is the difference between a number you can publish and a number that is a lie. This is Week 4's lesson revisited in the small-data EM context.
- EM anchor: "start with feature extraction" is the practical rule for the typical EM lab situation. With 30 labelled images and a ResNet-50 backbone, feature extraction (train only the head) avoids overfitting the backbone and gives a working model within minutes. Fine-tuning is the next step once the head has converged.
::::

## Putting it all together: 30 labelled TEM frames, 5 000 unlabelled

:::: {.incremental}
- **Step 0 — Split first:** assign specimens/sessions to train/validation/test *before* anything else; de-duplicate with embedding retrieval.
- **Step 1 — Pick a backbone:** frozen DINOv2 / μSAM encoder, or SimCLR/MAE pretraining on the 5 000 unlabelled frames, or synthetic pretraining (Voronoi, multislice) if the physics generator captures the task-relevant invariant.
- **Step 2 — Diagnose:** kNN neighbours, precision@k, 2-D map coloured by session; linear probe vs random-init baseline.
- **Step 3 — Adapt:** linear probe first; LP→fine-tune with differential learning rates only if it beats the probe on the grouped validation split. Augment throughout — physics gate on every transform.
- **Step 4 — Spend new labels wisely:** SAM-assisted annotation + active learning on the most uncertain / diverse frames; repeat Steps 3–4.
- **Step 5 — Report honestly:** IoU/Dice or accuracy on held-out specimens, with the protocol and N stated.
::::

:::: {.notes}
- This is the synthesis of the lecture — name it as such. Every step maps to a section of today.
- The U-Net and CNN architectures from Week 7 are unchanged. What changed is *how we initialise and train* them.
- The miniproject template: students with their own EM data should follow exactly these steps, using the notebook code as a starting point.
- Pacing: 3 minutes — high-value synthesis slide.
- Transition: "The notebook."
::::

## Summary: the week in six points

:::: {.incremental}
1. **Labels, not pixels, are the bottleneck** in EM; at $N\approx 50$ networks memorise shortcuts — diagnose with grouped validation and saliency.
2. **Augmentation encodes physical invariances** — each transform is a claim; illegal ones (EBSD rotation, DS flip, EELS intensity, zoom for size tasks) inject label noise or erase the signal.
3. **Transfer = backbone + new head:** feature extraction for few labels; fine-tuning with differential learning rates, gradual unfreezing or LP→FT against catastrophic forgetting.
4. **Synthetic data** gives perfect free labels; it transfers when the generator captures the task-relevant invariant and spans the imaging-condition nuisance distribution.
5. **Self-supervised learning** pretrains on the unlabelled mountain: SimCLR (InfoNCE, augmentations = labels), MAE (mask 75 %, reconstruct), DINO (EMA teacher, no negatives); foundation models (DINOv2, SAM/μSAM) usually need in-domain adaptation for EM.
6. **Evaluate embeddings** with linear probe, kNN retrieval/precision@k and nuisance-coloured maps — always against a random-init baseline and on specimen-grouped splits.
::::

:::: {.notes}
- Read out loud; ask students to name, for each point, the slide or notebook cell that demonstrated it.
- Transition: "The must-know list for the exam."
::::

## Must-know for the exam

:::: {.incremental}
- Why $N\approx 50$ labels + $10^7$ parameters overfits; train–val gap and Grad-CAM as shortcut diagnostics; **split by specimen first, then augment**.
- Augmentation legality: justify each transform by a physical symmetry; name an illegal case and why.
- Feature extraction vs fine-tuning decision (labels × domain gap); differential LRs ($\eta_\text{backbone}\ll\eta_\text{head}$) and why catastrophic forgetting happens.
- InfoNCE: $\ell_{i,j}=-\log\frac{\exp(\mathrm{sim}(\mathbf{z}_i,\mathbf{z}_j)/\tau)}{\sum_{k\neq i}\exp(\mathrm{sim}(\mathbf{z}_i,\mathbf{z}_k)/\tau)}$ — positives, negatives, temperature, chance level $\log(2N-1)$.
- Collapse and its remedies: negatives (SimCLR), reconstruction (MAE), EMA teacher + centring/sharpening (DINO).
- Linear probe vs LP→FT vs scratch: what each trains, when each wins; kNN retrieval with cosine similarity and precision@k.
::::

:::: {.notes}
- These mirror the written must-know list for Week 8 in the course exam document.
- Typical exam questions: design the augmentation set for a given EM task and justify it; write the InfoNCE loss and explain the role of $\tau$; interpret a label-efficiency plot like today's; explain why zero-shot SAM numbers on EM data are not the method's performance.
::::
